 Corporate Guarantees Attract GST, But 1% Valuation Is Not Mandatory: Delhi High Court
 Abhishek Raja 
 Abhishek Raja 
 Author 
 Follow 
 View profile 
 Last updated: 21 November 2026 
 Save 
 Share 
 Join Us 
 Follow Us 
 Add as Source 
 Executive Summary
 A parent's corporate guarantee to secure a related subsidiary's borrowing is a taxable supply under Schedule I, even without consideration.
 Rule 28(2) survives, but its 1% per annum value is not an irrebuttable minimum.
 A lower open-market value can be established through cogent evidence.
 Old guarantees are not repeatedly taxable merely because they continue after 26 October 2023.
 1. The Issue
 The petitions challenged GST on corporate guarantees furnished by holding companies for the borrowings of their subsidiaries and SPVs. The immediate controversy concerned Rule 28(2) of the CGST Rules, 2017, inserted from 26 October 2023 and later amended retrospectively to specify 1% per annum of the guaranteed amount, or actual consideration, whichever is higher.
 The petitioners contended that a gratuitous shareholder guarantee was not a "supply"; alternatively, it was a shareholder activity, not an independently taxable service. They also challenged the compulsory 1% floor, the retrospective amendment and the Department's premise that a continuing guarantee generated fresh annual supplies.
 The Court confined itself to corporate guarantees and Rule 28(2), leaving other challenges in certain connected petitions open (paragraph 4).
 2. Department's Arguments
 The Revenue argued that a corporate guarantee substitutes collateral or a bank guarantee, allows the subsidiary to obtain finance without blocking assets, and transfers credit support from the parent to the subsidiary. The holding company's legal undertaking therefore carried economic value.
 Because a holding company and subsidiary are related persons, the guarantee was taxable under Section 7(1)(c) read with Entry 2 of Schedule I, notwithstanding absence of consideration. The subsidiary, rather than the lender, was the recipient because its borrowing was secured and its access to credit enabled.
 On valuation, the Revenue submitted that related-party transactions fall outside Section 15(1). Rule 28(2), issued on GST Council recommendation, addressed the difficulty of determining comparables for intra-group guarantees. The 1% benchmark drew support from the transfer-pricing Safe Harbour Rules.
 3. Assessee's Arguments
 The assessee argued that the guarantee was given to protect the parent's investment, making it a shareholder activity rather than a supply in the course or furtherance of business. It relied on the absence of any guarantee fee and the distinction between explicit services and incidental benefits of group membership.
 It also submitted that Rule 28(2) imposed an arbitrary valuation disconnected from actual risk, creditworthiness, duration, collateral, probability of default and comparable third-party pricing. The phrase "whichever is higher" made the 1% figure an inflexible tax floor even where credible market evidence showed a lower value.
 The assessee further contended that a guarantee is a one-time undertaking, not a continuous supply. Consequently, a guarantee executed before 26 October 2023 could not be brought within Rule 28(2) merely because it remained alive thereafter.
 4. Holding and Reasoning
 The Court partly allowed the petitions.
 First, it held that an explicit corporate guarantee in favour of a subsidiary is a taxable supply under Section 7(1)(c) read with Entry 2 of Schedule I, even without consideration. The decisive feature was the assumption of a legally enforceable financial risk which supplied credit support to the subsidiary. A parent's investment-protection motive did not change the transaction's legal character (paragraphs 53–63). The Court treated the subsidiary as recipient under Section 2(93)(c), since the subsidiary's borrowing was secured and credit access enabled (paragraphs 64–65). indiankanoon. org
 Secondly, it upheld Rule 28(2) as intra vires Sections 15 and 164. However, it read down the 1% per annum figure: it is a default deemed value, not an unanswerable statutory minimum. The supplier may establish a lower open-market value through cogent and verifiable material. The agreed nil consideration, or a bare assertion that the parties are related, will not suffice (paragraphs 87, 91 and 123–124). indiankanoon. org
 Thirdly, the Court held that supply occurs on execution of the guarantee and again on renewal, extension or enhancement. It is not a continuous supply of services. The tax is computed for the guarantee tenure at execution; an early release may justify a credit note under Section 34, subject to statutory limits (paragraphs 92–100 and 125).
 Finally, guarantees executed between 1 July 2017 and 25 October 2023 remain taxable, but must be valued under the Rules then applicable; Rule 28(2) and its 1% figure cannot be imported into that period. Guarantees predating GST are outside the levy unless renewed, extended or enhanced thereafter. Rule 28(2) applies only to the relevant event on or after 26 October 2023 (paragraphs 126–127). indiankanoon. org
 5. Then and Now: The Pre-GST Lineage
 The valuation limb recalls Union of India v Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats Pvt. Ltd. , where the Supreme Court held that delegated valuation rules cannot outrun the charging and valuation provisions of the parent statute. The Delhi High Court did not invalidate Rule 28(2); Section 15 expressly permits prescribed valuation for notified supplies. Yet the same discipline operates at the constitutional level: a deemed value cannot be made immune from evidence of a lower market value where doing so becomes arbitrary.
 On circulars, the Court followed the older excise principle in Ratan Melting & Wire Industries : a Board circular binds departmental officers but cannot override statutory text or judicial interpretation. Thus, Circular Nos. 204 and 225 survive only insofar as they conform to the judgment.
 6. Allied Law Lens
 The Contract Act matters only for identifying the transaction's economic beneficiary. The Court used Section 127 to explain why the principal debtor benefits from the surety's undertaking; it did not treat that benefit as "consideration" under Section 2(31).
 Likewise, Ind AS 109 was corroborative, not constitutive. Accounting recognition of a financial guarantee at fair value may support a factual valuation analysis, but it cannot itself create GST liability (paragraphs 54–55).
 7. Analysis and Conclusion
 This is the most consequential corporate-guarantee judgment yet rendered under GST. It rejects the broad proposition that shareholder motive excludes an explicit guarantee from Schedule I. Equally, it prevents the 1% rule from becoming a statutory fiction detached from commercial reality.
 There is a material divergence from the Gujarat High Court's approach in Torrent Power Ltd. v Union of India . While Torrent Power treated continuing pre-26 October 2023 guarantees as attracting levy from that date, the Delhi High Court holds that continued existence alone is not a fresh supply. The conflict, coupled with the scale of group financing affected, makes Supreme Court scrutiny likely.
 The immediate controversy will shift from legal character to proof. The most litigated questions will be what constitutes credible open-market-value evidence, whether the subsidiary has full ITC eligibility, and whether a later amendment amounts to renewal, extension or enhancement.
 8. Practice Tips
 Create a guarantee register recording execution date, tenure, amount, borrower, lender, extensions, renewals, enhancements and discharge date.
 For guarantees after 26 October 2023, maintain a contemporaneous valuation file: credit rating, collateral, debt service, comparable bank quotations, risk analysis and transfer-pricing material.
 Do not assume that nil consideration proves nil value; it does not meet the Court's evidentiary threshold.
 Identify pre-26 October 2023 guarantees separately. Resist application of Rule 28(2) merely because an old instrument remained outstanding.
 For early release or discharge, evaluate a Section 34 credit note promptly, keeping its statutory time-limit in view.
 References 
 Sterlite Power Transmission Limited v Union of India , W.P.(C) No. 2966 of 2024 and connected matters, Delhi High Court, decided on 17 November 2026.
 Torrent Power Ltd. v Union of India , Gujarat High Court, decided on 14 August 2026.
 Union of India v Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats Pvt. Ltd. , (2018) 4 SCC 669.

 Notification No. 52/2023-Central Tax, dated 26 October 2023.
 Notification No. 12/2024-Central Tax, dated 10 July 2024.
 Circular No. 204/16/2023-GST, dated 27 October 2023.
